correctQuery: SELECT city_name, COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT city_name, humidity, DATE_TRUNC('month', reading_date) as mon, PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY humidity) OVER(PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC('month', reading_date)) as p25, PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY humidity) OVER(PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC('month', reading_date)) as p75 FROM weather_data) t WHERE humidity BETWEEN p25 AND p75 GROUP BY city_name;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE weather_data (city_name VARCHAR, reading_date DATE, humidity NUMERIC);

title: Sensor Coverage Gaps
scenario: Find cities that had at least one day without any sensor reporting data in the last 30 days.
tableSchema: weather_data (city_name VARCHAR, reading_date DATE)
hint: Compare actual reading days vs count of days in interval.
correctQuery: SELECT city_name FROM weather_data WHERE reading_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days' GROUP BY city_name HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT reading_date) < 30;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE weather_data (city_name VARCHAR, reading_date DATE);

title: Temperature Trend Persistence
scenario: Identify cities where the daily average temperature has been increasing for 5 consecutive days.
tableSchema: weather_data (city_name VARCHAR, reading_date DATE, temp_c NUMERIC)
hint: LAG(temp) vs temp, create groups, count streak.
correctQuery: SELECT city_name FROM (SELECT city_name, COUNT(*) as streak FROM (SELECT city_name, reading_date, (reading_date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY city_name ORDER BY reading_date)::INT) as grp FROM (SELECT city_name, reading_date, temp_c, LAG(temp_c) OVER(PARTITION BY city_name ORDER BY reading_date) as prev_temp FROM weather_data) t WHERE temp_c > prev_temp) t2 GROUP BY city_name, grp) t3 WHERE streak >= 5;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE weather_data (city_name VARCHAR, reading_date DATE, temp_c NUMERIC);

title: Peak Alert Duration
scenario: For cities with repeated alerts, calculate the average time between the end of one alert and the start of the next.
tableSchema: climate_alerts (city_name VARCHAR, alert_time TIMESTAMP)
hint: Use LEAD() to find next alert time.
correctQuery: SELECT city_name, AVG(next_time - alert_time) FROM (SELECT city_name, alert_time, LEAD(alert_time) OVER(PARTITION BY city_name ORDER BY alert_time) as next_time FROM climate_alerts) t GROUP BY city_name;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE climate_alerts (city_name VARCHAR, alert_time TIMESTAMP);

title: Model Performance Comparison
scenario: Find sensor models that have a lower average alert rate than the global model average.
tableSchema: sensor_registry (model_name VARCHAR, sensor_id INT), climate_alerts (sensor_id INT)
hint: Subquery for global avg, compare with group by.
correctQuery: SELECT model_name FROM (SELECT r.model_name, COUNT(a.sensor_id)::NUMERIC / COUNT(DISTINCT r.sensor_id) as alert_rate FROM sensor_registry r LEFT JOIN climate_alerts a ON r.sensor_id = a.sensor_id GROUP BY r.model_name) t WHERE alert_rate < (SELECT AVG(rate) FROM (SELECT COUNT(a2.sensor_id)::NUMERIC / COUNT(DISTINCT r2.sensor_id) as rate FROM sensor_registry r2 LEFT JOIN climate_alerts a2 ON r2.sensor_id = a2.sensor_id GROUP BY r2.model_name) t2);
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE sensor_registry (model_name VARCHAR, sensor_id INT); CREATE TABLE climate_alerts (sensor_id INT);

title: Diverging Weather Patterns
scenario: Find cities whose temperature deviation from the annual mean has tripled in the last year compared to the historical average.
tableSchema: weather_data (city_name VARCHAR, reading_date DATE, temp_c NUMERIC)
hint: Compare last-year-stddev vs historical-stddev.
correctQuery: SELECT city_name FROM (SELECT city_name, STDDEV(temp_c) FILTER (WHERE reading_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 year') as last_year_sd, STDDEV(temp_c) FILTER (WHERE reading_date < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 year') as hist_sd FROM weather_data GROUP BY city_name) t WHERE last_year_sd > 3 * hist_sd;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE weather_data (city_name VARCHAR, reading_date DATE, temp_c NUMERIC);

title: Sensor Reporting Density
scenario: Calculate the moving 7-day average of sensor reading counts per city to find reporting density.
tableSchema: weather_data (city_name VARCHAR, reading_date DATE)
hint: Count readings per city/date, then use AVG() OVER ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING.
correctQuery: SELECT city_name, reading_date, AVG(daily_count) OVER(PARTITION BY city_name ORDER BY reading_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) as density FROM (SELECT city_name, reading_date, COUNT(*) as daily_count FROM weather_data GROUP BY city_name, reading_date) t;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE weather_data (city_name VARCHAR, reading_date DATE);

title: Mean Time to Resolve (MTTR)
scenario: Calculate the average time (in hours) between a bug's creation and its transition to 'Resolved' status.
tableSchema: bugs (bug_id INT, created_at TIMESTAMP), status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Join bugs with history where status = 'Resolved', then find difference.
correctQuery: SELECT AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (sh.changed_at - b.created_at))/3600) as avg_mttr FROM bugs b JOIN status_history sh ON b.bug_id = sh.bug_id WHERE sh.status = 'Resolved';
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE bugs (bug_id INT, created_at TIMESTAMP); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Bug Reopen Frequency
scenario: Identify bugs that transitioned from 'Resolved' back to 'Open' more than twice.
tableSchema: status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Use LEAD() to check if status transitions match the 'Resolved' -> 'Open' pattern.
correctQuery: SELECT bug_id FROM (SELECT bug_id, status, LEAD(status) OVER(PARTITION BY bug_id ORDER BY changed_at) as next_status FROM status_history) t WHERE status = 'Resolved' AND next_status = 'Open' GROUP BY bug_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Sprint Velocity Stability
scenario: Find developers who have a lower than average bug-fix count compared to their team for three consecutive sprints.
tableSchema: developers (dev_id INT, team_id INT), status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP), sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE)
hint: Calculate fix counts per dev per sprint, then use window avg.
correctQuery: SELECT dev_id FROM (SELECT dev_id, sprint_id, fix_count, AVG(fix_count) OVER(PARTITION BY team_id, sprint_id) as team_avg, LAG(fix_count) OVER(PARTITION BY dev_id ORDER BY sprint_id) as prev_fix FROM (SELECT d.dev_id, d.team_id, s.sprint_id, COUNT(*) as fix_count FROM developers d JOIN status_history sh ON d.dev_id = sh.bug_id JOIN sprints s ON sh.changed_at::DATE BETWEEN s.start_date AND s.end_date WHERE sh.status = 'Resolved' GROUP BY d.dev_id, d.team_id, s.sprint_id) t) t2 WHERE fix_count < team_avg AND prev_fix < team_avg;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE developers (dev_id INT, team_id INT); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP); CREATE TABLE sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE);

title: Severity Escalation Latency
scenario: Calculate the average time elapsed between a bug being created and its severity being upgraded (e.g., Medium to High).
tableSchema: bugs (bug_id INT, severity VARCHAR, created_at TIMESTAMP), status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Self-join or use lead/lag on history.
correctQuery: SELECT AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (sh.changed_at - b.created_at))/3600) FROM bugs b JOIN status_history sh ON b.bug_id = sh.bug_id WHERE b.severity = 'Medium' AND sh.status = 'Escalated_High';
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE bugs (bug_id INT, severity VARCHAR, created_at TIMESTAMP); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Bottleneck Analysis
scenario: For each status, find the average time a bug stays in that state before transitioning to the next state.
tableSchema: status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Use LEAD() to find the timestamp of the next status change.
correctQuery: SELECT status, AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (next_changed_at - changed_at))/3600) FROM (SELECT status, changed_at, LEAD(changed_at) OVER(PARTITION BY bug_id ORDER BY changed_at) as next_changed_at FROM status_history) t GROUP BY status;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Developer Burnout Prediction
scenario: Identify developers who handled more than 50% of the team's bug load in any single sprint.
tableSchema: developers (dev_id INT, team_id INT), status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP), sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE)
hint: Window partition by sprint and team.
correctQuery: SELECT dev_id FROM (SELECT dev_id, sprint_id, COUNT(*) as dev_load, SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER(PARTITION BY team_id, sprint_id) as team_load FROM developers d JOIN status_history sh ON d.dev_id = sh.bug_id JOIN sprints s ON sh.changed_at::DATE BETWEEN s.start_date AND s.end_date GROUP BY dev_id, team_id, sprint_id) t WHERE dev_load::NUMERIC / team_load > 0.5;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE developers (dev_id INT, team_id INT); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP); CREATE TABLE sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE);

title: Sprint Overlap Issues
scenario: Find bugs that were reported in one sprint but not resolved until three sprints later.
tableSchema: bugs (bug_id INT, created_at TIMESTAMP), status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP), sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE)
hint: Join bugs and resolved status with sprint start/end dates.
correctQuery: SELECT b.bug_id FROM bugs b JOIN status_history sh ON b.bug_id = sh.bug_id JOIN sprints s1 ON b.created_at::DATE BETWEEN s1.start_date AND s1.end_date JOIN sprints s2 ON sh.changed_at::DATE BETWEEN s2.start_date AND s2.end_date WHERE sh.status = 'Resolved' AND s2.sprint_id >= s1.sprint_id + 3;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE bugs (bug_id INT, created_at TIMESTAMP); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP); CREATE TABLE sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE);

title: Severity Shift Correlation
scenario: Calculate the correlation between the number of times a bug status changes and the eventual severity level.
tableSchema: bugs (bug_id INT, severity VARCHAR), status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR)
hint: Count history entries per bug and group by severity.
correctQuery: SELECT severity, AVG(change_count) FROM (SELECT b.severity, b.bug_id, COUNT(sh.status) as change_count FROM bugs b JOIN status_history sh ON b.bug_id = sh.bug_id GROUP BY b.severity, b.bug_id) t GROUP BY severity;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE bugs (bug_id INT, severity VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR);

title: Rapid-Fix Sprints
scenario: Identify sprints where the MTTR was 20% lower than the rolling 3-sprint average.
tableSchema: sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE), status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Calculate MTTR per sprint, then use AVG() OVER (ROWS 3 PRECEDING).
correctQuery: SELECT sprint_id FROM (SELECT sprint_id, mttr, AVG(mttr) OVER(ORDER BY sprint_id ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) as prev_avg FROM (SELECT sprint_id, AVG(...) as mttr FROM sprints s JOIN status_history sh ON ...) t) t2 WHERE mttr < 0.8 * prev_avg;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Bug Density by Reporter
scenario: Find reporters whose reported bugs have the highest average time-to-resolution, signaling possible complex bug reporting.
tableSchema: bugs (bug_id INT, reporter_id INT), status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Calculate TTR per bug, then average by reporter.
correctQuery: SELECT reporter_id, AVG(ttr) as avg_ttr FROM (SELECT b.reporter_id, b.bug_id, MAX(sh.changed_at) - MIN(b.created_at) as ttr FROM bugs b JOIN status_history sh ON b.bug_id = sh.bug_id GROUP BY b.reporter_id, b.bug_id) t GROUP BY reporter_id ORDER BY avg_ttr DESC;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE bugs (bug_id INT, reporter_id INT); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Stale Bug Detection
scenario: Find bugs that have been in 'In Progress' status for longer than the 90th percentile of all 'In Progress' durations.
tableSchema: status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Use PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) to set threshold.
correctQuery: SELECT bug_id FROM (SELECT bug_id, status, changed_at, LEAD(changed_at) OVER(PARTITION BY bug_id ORDER BY changed_at) - changed_at as duration FROM status_history WHERE status = 'In_Progress') t WHERE duration > (SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY LEAD(changed_at) OVER(PARTITION BY bug_id ORDER BY changed_at) - changed_at) FROM status_history WHERE status = 'In_Progress');
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Team Workload Skew
scenario: Identify teams where the standard deviation of bug-fix counts across developers is higher than the company-wide average.
tableSchema: developers (dev_id INT, team_id INT), status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR)
hint: Calculate dev-counts, group by team for SD, compare to global average.
correctQuery: SELECT team_id FROM (SELECT team_id, STDDEV(fix_count) as team_sd FROM (SELECT team_id, dev_id, COUNT(*) as fix_count FROM developers JOIN status_history ON dev_id = bug_id GROUP BY team_id, dev_id) t GROUP BY team_id) t2 WHERE team_sd > (SELECT AVG(sd) FROM (SELECT team_id, STDDEV(fix_count) as sd FROM ... GROUP BY team_id) t3);
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE developers (dev_id INT, team_id INT); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR);

title: Critical Bug Lifecycle
scenario: Compare the duration of the first status change to the duration of the last status change for 'Critical' bugs.
tableSchema: bugs (bug_id INT, severity VARCHAR), status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Rank history entries per bug.
correctQuery: SELECT bug_id, (last_dur - first_dur) FROM (SELECT bug_id, MIN(duration) FILTER (WHERE rnk=1) as first_dur, MAX(duration) FILTER (WHERE rnk_desc=1) as last_dur FROM (SELECT bug_id, changed_at - LAG(changed_at) OVER(PARTITION BY bug_id ORDER BY changed_at) as duration, RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY bug_id ORDER BY changed_at) as rnk, RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY bug_id ORDER BY changed_at DESC) as rnk_desc FROM status_history) t GROUP BY bug_id) t2;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE bugs (bug_id INT, severity VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Bug Resolution Clustering
scenario: Find dates where more than 5 bugs were resolved within the same 1-hour window.
tableSchema: status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Use window function with range frame.
correctQuery: SELECT changed_at FROM (SELECT changed_at, COUNT(*) OVER(ORDER BY changed_at RANGE BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND INTERVAL '1 hour' FOLLOWING) as bug_burst FROM status_history WHERE status = 'Resolved') t WHERE bug_burst > 5;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Developer Specialization
scenario: Find developers who resolve 80% of their bugs in a single specific severity category.
tableSchema: developers (dev_id INT), bugs (bug_id INT, severity VARCHAR), status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR)
hint: Group by dev and severity, use count over partition.
correctQuery: SELECT dev_id FROM (SELECT dev_id, severity, COUNT(*)::NUMERIC / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER(PARTITION BY dev_id) as pct FROM developers JOIN bugs ON dev_id = reporter_id JOIN status_history ON bugs.bug_id = status_history.bug_id WHERE status = 'Resolved' GROUP BY dev_id, severity) t WHERE pct > 0.8;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE developers (dev_id INT); CREATE TABLE bugs (bug_id INT, severity VARCHAR, reporter_id INT); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR);

title: Sprint Overload Threshold
scenario: Find sprints where the cumulative severity score of bugs exceeded 100 before the midpoint of the sprint.
tableSchema: bugs (bug_id INT, severity VARCHAR), status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP), sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE)
hint: Map severity to numeric (10, 50, 100), then running total.
correctQuery: SELECT sprint_id FROM (SELECT sprint_id, changed_at, SUM(CASE severity WHEN 'High' THEN 100 WHEN 'Medium' THEN 50 ELSE 10 END) OVER(PARTITION BY sprint_id ORDER BY changed_at) as cum_sev FROM bugs b JOIN status_history sh ON b.bug_id = sh.bug_id JOIN sprints s ON sh.changed_at::DATE BETWEEN s.start_date AND s.end_date) t WHERE cum_sev > 100 AND changed_at < (SELECT start_date + (end_date - start_date)/2 FROM sprints);
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE bugs (bug_id INT, severity VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, changed_at TIMESTAMP); CREATE TABLE sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE);

title: Incident Response Lag
scenario: Identify incidents where the time between bug report and the first 'In_Progress' state is greater than the rolling average of the last 10 incidents.
tableSchema: bugs (bug_id INT, created_at TIMESTAMP), status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Calculate duration, then compare with AVG() OVER ROWS 10 PRECEDING.
correctQuery: SELECT bug_id FROM (SELECT bug_id, duration, AVG(duration) OVER(ORDER BY created_at ROWS BETWEEN 10 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) as roll_avg FROM (SELECT b.bug_id, b.created_at, MIN(sh.changed_at) - b.created_at as duration FROM bugs b JOIN status_history sh ON b.bug_id = sh.bug_id WHERE sh.status = 'In_Progress' GROUP BY b.bug_id, b.created_at) t) t2 WHERE duration > roll_avg;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE bugs (bug_id INT, created_at TIMESTAMP); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Bug Resolution Velocity
scenario: Find developers whose monthly resolution count has increased every month for the last 6 months.
tableSchema: developers (dev_id INT), status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Count resolved bugs per month, compare using LAGs or window frame.
correctQuery: SELECT dev_id FROM (SELECT dev_id, mon, cnt, LAG(cnt, 1) OVER(PARTITION BY dev_id ORDER BY mon) as p1, ... FROM (SELECT dev_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', changed_at) as mon, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM developers JOIN status_history ON dev_id = bug_id WHERE status = 'Resolved' GROUP BY dev_id, mon) t) t2 WHERE cnt > p1 AND p1 > p2 AND p2 > p3 AND p3 > p4 AND p4 > p5;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE developers (dev_id INT); CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Peak Workload Distribution
scenario: Find the peak hour of bug reporting for each team and identify if it aligns with their highest MTTR.
tableSchema: developers (dev_id INT, team_id INT), bugs (bug_id INT, reporter_id INT, created_at TIMESTAMP)
hint: Aggregate by team/hour, then rank.
correctQuery: SELECT team_id, report_hour FROM (SELECT team_id, EXTRACT(HOUR FROM created_at) as report_hour, COUNT(*), RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY team_id ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) as rnk FROM developers d JOIN bugs b ON d.dev_id = b.reporter_id GROUP BY team_id, report_hour) t WHERE rnk = 1;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE developers (dev_id INT, team_id INT); CREATE TABLE bugs (bug_id INT, reporter_id INT, created_at TIMESTAMP);

title: Sprint Progress Velocity
scenario: Calculate the percentage of total sprint bugs resolved per day, and identify days where resolution fell below 5% of total.
tableSchema: status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP), sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE)
hint: Divide daily count by total count per sprint.
correctQuery: SELECT sprint_id, changed_at::DATE FROM (SELECT s.sprint_id, sh.changed_at, COUNT(*) OVER(PARTITION BY s.sprint_id, sh.changed_at::DATE)::NUMERIC / COUNT(*) OVER(PARTITION BY s.sprint_id) as daily_pct FROM status_history sh JOIN sprints s ON sh.changed_at::DATE BETWEEN s.start_date AND s.end_date WHERE sh.status = 'Resolved') t WHERE daily_pct < 0.05;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE status_history (bug_id INT, status VARCHAR, changed_at TIMESTAMP); CREATE TABLE sprints (sprint_id INT, start_date DATE, end_date DATE);

title: Article Viral Velocity
scenario: Identify articles where the page views in a single day exceeded the article's 7-day rolling average by more than 300%.
tableSchema: page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT)
hint: Use AVG(views_count) OVER (...) with a range frame.
correctQuery: SELECT article_id, view_date FROM (SELECT article_id, view_date, views_count, AVG(views_count) OVER(PARTITION BY article_id ORDER BY view_date ROWS BETWEEN 7 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) as avg_7d FROM page_views) t WHERE views_count > 3 * avg_7d;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT);

title: Author Content Consistency
scenario: For each author, find the longest consecutive streak of days they published at least one article.
tableSchema: articles (author_id INT, publish_date DATE)
hint: Create groups by subtracting row number from date.
correctQuery: SELECT author_id, MAX(streak) FROM (SELECT author_id, COUNT(*) as streak FROM (SELECT author_id, publish_date, (publish_date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY author_id ORDER BY publish_date)::INT) as grp FROM (SELECT DISTINCT author_id, publish_date FROM articles) t) t2 GROUP BY author_id, grp) t3 GROUP BY author_id;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (author_id INT, publish_date DATE);

title: Category Engagement Saturation
scenario: Identify the top 3 categories by comment density (comments per article) for each month.
tableSchema: articles (article_id INT, category_id INT, publish_date DATE), comments (comment_id INT, article_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP)
hint: Join and partition by month.
correctQuery: SELECT mon, category_id FROM (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', c.comment_date) as mon, a.category_id, COUNT(c.comment_id)::NUMERIC / COUNT(DISTINCT a.article_id) as density, RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC('month', c.comment_date) ORDER BY COUNT(c.comment_id)::NUMERIC / COUNT(DISTINCT a.article_id) DESC) as rnk FROM articles a JOIN comments c ON a.article_id = c.article_id GROUP BY mon, a.category_id) t WHERE rnk <= 3;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, category_id INT, publish_date DATE); CREATE TABLE comments (comment_id INT, article_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP);

title: Comment Sentiment Lag
scenario: Find articles where the average time between consecutive comments has decreased by 50% compared to the previous week.
tableSchema: comments (article_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP)
hint: Calculate comment intervals using LAG(), then aggregate by week.
correctQuery: SELECT article_id FROM (SELECT article_id, week, avg_int, LAG(avg_int) OVER(PARTITION BY article_id ORDER BY week) as prev_avg FROM (SELECT article_id, DATE_TRUNC('week', comment_date) as week, AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (comment_date - LAG(comment_date) OVER(PARTITION BY article_id ORDER BY comment_date)))) as avg_int FROM comments GROUP BY article_id, week) t) t2 WHERE avg_int < 0.5 * prev_avg;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE comments (article_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP);

title: Author Burnout Signal
scenario: Flag authors whose article output has decreased for 3 consecutive months.
tableSchema: articles (author_id INT, publish_date DATE)
hint: Use LAG() to compare counts.
correctQuery: SELECT author_id FROM (SELECT author_id, mon, cnt, LAG(cnt) OVER(PARTITION BY author_id ORDER BY mon) as p1, LAG(cnt, 2) OVER(PARTITION BY author_id ORDER BY mon) as p2 FROM (SELECT author_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', publish_date) as mon, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM articles GROUP BY author_id, mon) t) t2 WHERE cnt < p1 AND p1 < p2;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (author_id INT, publish_date DATE);

title: High-Dwell Content
scenario: Find articles where the dwell time is 2 standard deviations above the category average.
tableSchema: articles (article_id INT, category_id INT), page_views (article_id INT, duration_seconds INT)
hint: Use AVG() OVER(PARTITION BY category_id) and STDDEV().
correctQuery: SELECT article_id FROM (SELECT article_id, duration_seconds, AVG(duration_seconds) OVER(PARTITION BY category_id) as avg_d, STDDEV(duration_seconds) OVER(PARTITION BY category_id) as std_d FROM articles JOIN page_views USING (article_id)) t WHERE duration_seconds > avg_d + 2 * std_d;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, category_id INT); CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, duration_seconds INT);

title: Category Lifecycle Tracking
scenario: Track the evolution of category popularity by finding consecutive months where view counts increased.
tableSchema: page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT), articles (article_id INT, category_id INT)
hint: Group views by category/month, then use LAG().
correctQuery: SELECT category_id, mon FROM (SELECT category_id, mon, views, LAG(views) OVER(PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY mon) as prev FROM (SELECT a.category_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', p.view_date) as mon, SUM(p.views_count) as views FROM articles a JOIN page_views p USING (article_id) GROUP BY a.category_id, mon) t) t2 WHERE views > prev;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT); CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, category_id INT);

title: Top Author Contribution Delta
scenario: Find authors who contributed to the Top 10 viewed articles in two consecutive months.
tableSchema: articles (article_id INT, author_id INT), page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT)
hint: Rank articles by views per month, filter top 10, then join with self on author.
correctQuery: SELECT author_id FROM (SELECT author_id, mon, RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY mon ORDER BY views DESC) as rnk FROM (SELECT a.author_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', p.view_date) as mon, SUM(p.views_count) as views FROM articles a JOIN page_views p USING (article_id) GROUP BY a.author_id, mon) t) t2 WHERE rnk <= 10 GROUP BY author_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT mon) >= 2;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, author_id INT); CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT);

title: Comment Frequency Spike
scenario: Identify articles that received a comment burst (3x their rolling 30-day average) on any given day.
tableSchema: comments (article_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP)
hint: Aggregate daily, compute 30-day moving average.
correctQuery: SELECT article_id FROM (SELECT article_id, day, daily_cnt, AVG(daily_cnt) OVER(PARTITION BY article_id ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '30 days' PRECEDING AND INTERVAL '1 day' PRECEDING) as roll_avg FROM (SELECT article_id, comment_date::DATE as day, COUNT(*) as daily_cnt FROM comments GROUP BY article_id, day) t) t2 WHERE daily_cnt > 3 * roll_avg;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE comments (article_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP);

title: Content Decay Analysis
scenario: Calculate the half-life of an article (days until views drop to 50% of the maximum daily views observed).
tableSchema: page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT)
hint: Find max views, then locate the first day after peak where views <= max/2.
correctQuery: SELECT article_id, MIN(view_date) - peak_date as half_life_days FROM (SELECT article_id, view_date, views_count, MAX(views_count) OVER(PARTITION BY article_id) as max_v, MAX(view_date) FILTER (WHERE views_count = MAX(views_count) OVER(PARTITION BY article_id)) OVER(PARTITION BY article_id) as peak_date FROM page_views) t WHERE views_count <= max_v * 0.5 AND view_date > peak_date GROUP BY article_id, peak_date;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT);

title: Category Diversity per Author
scenario: Find authors who have published in at least 5 different categories and have an average of > 100 views per article.
tableSchema: articles (article_id INT, author_id INT, category_id INT), page_views (article_id INT, views_count INT)
hint: Group by author, count categories, then average views.
correctQuery: SELECT author_id FROM (SELECT author_id, COUNT(DISTINCT category_id) as cat_count, AVG(total_views) as avg_views FROM (SELECT author_id, category_id, article_id, SUM(views_count) as total_views FROM articles JOIN page_views USING (article_id) GROUP BY author_id, category_id, article_id) t GROUP BY author_id) t2 WHERE cat_count >= 5 AND avg_views > 100;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, author_id INT, category_id INT); CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, views_count INT);

title: Commenter Engagement Depth
scenario: Calculate the average time a user spends commenting across different articles.
tableSchema: comments (user_id INT, article_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP)
hint: Sort by user then date, use LAG().
correctQuery: SELECT user_id, AVG(time_diff) FROM (SELECT user_id, comment_date - LAG(comment_date) OVER(PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY comment_date) as time_diff FROM comments) t GROUP BY user_id;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE comments (user_id INT, article_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP);

title: Category Virality Trend
scenario: Find categories where the total views have consistently increased for 4 consecutive months.
tableSchema: categories (category_id INT), articles (article_id INT, category_id INT), page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT)
hint: Aggregate by month, compare using LAG().
correctQuery: SELECT category_id FROM (SELECT category_id, mon, v, LAG(v) OVER(PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY mon) as l1, LAG(v, 2) OVER(PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY mon) as l2, LAG(v, 3) OVER(PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY mon) as l3 FROM (SELECT c.category_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', p.view_date) as mon, SUM(p.views_count) as v FROM categories c JOIN articles a USING (category_id) JOIN page_views p USING (article_id) GROUP BY c.category_id, mon) t) t2 WHERE v > l1 AND l1 > l2 AND l2 > l3;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE categories (category_id INT); CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, category_id INT); CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT);

title: Article View Distribution
scenario: Identify articles in the Top 10% of total views per category.
tableSchema: articles (article_id INT, category_id INT), page_views (article_id INT, views_count INT)
hint: Use PERCENT_RANK().
correctQuery: SELECT article_id FROM (SELECT article_id, PERCENT_RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY SUM(views_count) DESC) as pr FROM articles JOIN page_views USING (article_id) GROUP BY article_id, category_id) t WHERE pr <= 0.1;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, category_id INT); CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, views_count INT);

title: Author Response Latency
scenario: Calculate the average time authors take to comment on their own articles.
tableSchema: articles (article_id INT, author_id INT), comments (article_id INT, user_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP)
hint: Join comments with articles where user_id = author_id.
correctQuery: SELECT author_id, AVG(comment_date - publish_date) FROM articles a JOIN comments c ON a.article_id = c.article_id AND a.author_id = c.user_id GROUP BY author_id;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, author_id INT); CREATE TABLE comments (article_id INT, user_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP);

title: Commenter Network Expansion
scenario: Find users who have commented on at least 10 different categories.
tableSchema: articles (article_id INT, category_id INT), comments (comment_id INT, article_id INT, user_id INT)
hint: Count distinct categories per user.
correctQuery: SELECT user_id FROM comments c JOIN articles a USING (article_id) GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.category_id) >= 10;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, category_id INT); CREATE TABLE comments (comment_id INT, article_id INT, user_id INT);

title: Category View Concentration
scenario: Find articles that account for > 50% of their category's total monthly views.
tableSchema: articles (article_id INT, category_id INT), page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT)
hint: Calculate total views per category/month, then partition.
correctQuery: SELECT article_id FROM (SELECT article_id, SUM(views_count)::NUMERIC / SUM(SUM(views_count)) OVER(PARTITION BY category_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', view_date)) as pct FROM articles JOIN page_views USING (article_id) GROUP BY article_id, category_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', view_date)) t WHERE pct > 0.5;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, category_id INT); CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT);

title: Author Productivity Quartiles
scenario: Assign authors to productivity quartiles based on their total articles published.
tableSchema: articles (author_id INT, article_id INT)
hint: Use NTILE(4).
correctQuery: SELECT author_id, NTILE(4) OVER(ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) as quartile FROM articles GROUP BY author_id;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (author_id INT, article_id INT);

title: Page View Seasonality
scenario: Identify categories where views in the last quarter were significantly different (>= 50%) from the previous quarter.
tableSchema: categories (category_id INT), articles (article_id INT, category_id INT), page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT)
hint: Compare sums per quarter using LAG().
correctQuery: SELECT category_id FROM (SELECT category_id, qtr, sum_v, LAG(sum_v) OVER(PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY qtr) as prev_q FROM (SELECT category_id, DATE_TRUNC('quarter', view_date) as qtr, SUM(views_count) as sum_v FROM articles JOIN page_views USING (article_id) GROUP BY category_id, qtr) t) t2 WHERE ABS(sum_v - prev_q) / prev_q >= 0.5;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE categories (category_id INT); CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, category_id INT); CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT);

title: Article Comment Velocity
scenario: Calculate the moving 3-day average of comment volume per article.
tableSchema: comments (article_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP)
hint: Use ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
correctQuery: SELECT article_id, day, AVG(cnt) OVER(PARTITION BY article_id ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM (SELECT article_id, comment_date::DATE as day, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM comments GROUP BY article_id, day) t;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE comments (article_id INT, comment_date TIMESTAMP);

title: Recursive Content Virality Chains
scenario: Identify 'viral chains' where an article has at least 5 consecutive hours where the hourly view count is higher than the previous hour, recursively traversing the chain.
tableSchema: page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, hour_val INT, views_count INT)
hint: Use a Recursive CTE to build paths of hourly growth.
correctQuery: WITH RECURSIVE growth_chain AS (SELECT article_id, view_date, hour_val, 1 as chain_len FROM page_views p1 WHERE views_count > (SELECT views_count FROM page_views p2 WHERE p2.article_id = p1.article_id AND p2.hour_val = p1.hour_val - 1) UNION ALL SELECT pv.article_id, pv.view_date, pv.hour_val, gc.chain_len + 1 FROM page_views pv JOIN growth_chain gc ON pv.article_id = gc.article_id AND pv.hour_val = gc.hour_val + 1 WHERE pv.views_count > (SELECT views_count FROM page_views WHERE article_id = pv.article_id AND hour_val = pv.hour_val - 1)) SELECT article_id FROM growth_chain WHERE chain_len >= 5;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, hour_val INT, views_count INT);

title: Sentiment Reversal Detection
scenario: Identify articles where the aggregate sentiment score of comments reversed polarity (from positive > 0 to negative < 0) within a 24-hour window.
tableSchema: comments (article_id INT, sentiment_score NUMERIC, comment_date TIMESTAMP)
hint: Use AVG(sentiment_score) FILTER (WHERE...) and window frames.
correctQuery: SELECT article_id FROM (SELECT article_id, AVG(sentiment_score) OVER w_pos as avg_pos, AVG(sentiment_score) OVER w_neg as avg_neg FROM comments WINDOW w_pos AS (PARTITION BY article_id ORDER BY comment_date RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '24 hours' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), w_neg AS (PARTITION BY article_id ORDER BY comment_date RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '24 hours' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)) t WHERE avg_pos > 0 AND avg_neg < 0;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE comments (article_id INT, sentiment_score NUMERIC, comment_date TIMESTAMP);

title: Complex Author Contribution Peaks
scenario: Find authors whose total article view count in a rolling 7-day period is in the 99th percentile of all authors, calculated using a sliding range frame.
tableSchema: articles (author_id INT, article_id INT), page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT)
hint: Use PERCENTILE_CONT(0.99) OVER().
correctQuery: SELECT author_id FROM (SELECT author_id, SUM(views_count) OVER(PARTITION BY author_id ORDER BY view_date RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) as rolling_sum FROM articles JOIN page_views USING (article_id)) t WHERE rolling_sum > (SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.99) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY rolling_sum) FROM (SELECT SUM(views_count) OVER(PARTITION BY author_id ORDER BY view_date RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) as rolling_sum FROM articles JOIN page_views USING (article_id)) t2);
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (author_id INT, article_id INT); CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT);

title: Category Cannibalization
scenario: Detect when a new article release in a category causes a > 40% drop in views for existing articles in that same category within 48 hours.
tableSchema: articles (article_id INT, category_id INT, publish_date DATE), page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT)
hint: Use a lateral join to find the release event, then compare view aggregates.
correctQuery: SELECT a1.category_id, a1.article_id FROM articles a1 JOIN articles a2 ON a1.category_id = a2.category_id AND a2.publish_date BETWEEN a1.publish_date AND a1.publish_date + INTERVAL '2 days' WHERE a1.article_id != a2.article_id GROUP BY a1.category_id, a1.article_id HAVING SUM(a2.views_count) < 0.6 * SUM(a1.views_count);
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT, category_id INT, publish_date DATE); CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, view_date DATE, views_count INT);

title: Multi-Factor Engagement Score
scenario: Create a normalized 'Engagement Score' for articles where (Views * 0.7 + Comments * 0.3) is z-scored across the entire platform.
tableSchema: articles (article_id INT), page_views (article_id INT, views_count INT), comments (article_id INT, comment_id INT)
hint: Calculate aggregate per article, then apply (val - avg) / stddev.
correctQuery: WITH article_stats AS (SELECT article_id, (SUM(v.views_count) * 0.7 + COUNT(c.comment_id) * 0.3) as raw_score FROM articles a LEFT JOIN page_views v USING (article_id) LEFT JOIN comments c USING (article_id) GROUP BY article_id) SELECT article_id, (raw_score - AVG(raw_score) OVER()) / NULLIF(STDDEV(raw_score) OVER(), 0) as z_score FROM article_stats;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE articles (article_id INT); CREATE TABLE page_views (article_id INT, views_count INT); CREATE TABLE comments (article_id INT, comment_id INT);

title: LMS Course Completion Momentum
scenario: Identify students who finished a certificate faster than the rolling 3-certificate average of their peers, specifically within a 30-day window.
tableSchema: progress (stu_id INT, lesson_id INT, completion_date DATE), certificates (stu_id INT, issue_date DATE)
hint: Use a CTE to calculate individual duration and a windowed AVG() to determine peer benchmark.
correctQuery: WITH cert_times AS (SELECT stu_id, issue_date, (issue_date - MIN(completion_date) OVER(PARTITION BY stu_id)) as duration FROM certificates JOIN progress USING (stu_id)) SELECT stu_id FROM (SELECT stu_id, duration, AVG(duration) OVER(ORDER BY issue_date ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) as peer_avg FROM cert_times) t WHERE duration < peer_avg;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE progress (stu_id INT, lesson_id INT, completion_date DATE); CREATE TABLE certificates (cert_id INT, stu_id INT, issue_date DATE);

title: Music Playlist Engagement Drift
scenario: Detect 'genre fatigue': find songs whose addition-to-playlist rate has dropped by 50% compared to the genre's rolling 14-day average.
tableSchema: songs (song_id INT, genre_id INT), playlists (list_id INT, song_id INT, added_date TIMESTAMP)
hint: Aggregate daily, compute rolling average using RANGE intervals.
correctQuery: WITH daily_adds AS (SELECT song_id, genre_id, added_date::DATE as d, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM playlists JOIN songs USING (song_id) GROUP BY 1, 2, 3) SELECT song_id FROM (SELECT song_id, cnt, AVG(cnt) OVER(PARTITION BY genre_id ORDER BY d RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '14 days' PRECEDING AND INTERVAL '1 day' PRECEDING) as roll_avg FROM daily_adds) t WHERE cnt < 0.5 * roll_avg;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE songs (song_id INT, genre_id INT); CREATE TABLE playlists (list_id INT, song_id INT, added_date TIMESTAMP);

title: LMS Quiz Mastery Retention
scenario: Find students who scored > 90 on all quizzes taken in a sequence of at least 5 quizzes.
tableSchema: progress (stu_id INT, score INT, completion_date DATE)
hint: Create islands of success by partitioning and comparing ranks.
correctQuery: SELECT stu_id FROM (SELECT stu_id, COUNT(*) as streak FROM (SELECT stu_id, completion_date, (ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY stu_id ORDER BY completion_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY stu_id, CASE WHEN score > 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END ORDER BY completion_date)) as grp FROM progress) t WHERE score > 90 GROUP BY stu_id, grp) t2 WHERE streak >= 5;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE progress (stu_id INT, score INT, completion_date DATE);

title: Artist Playlist Dominance Transition
scenario: Identify the top 3 artists by playlist adds each month, then find artists who moved up in rank for 3 consecutive months.
tableSchema: artists (art_id INT), songs (song_id INT, art_id INT), playlists (list_id INT, song_id INT, added_date TIMESTAMP)
hint: Rank monthly, then use LAG to compare rank positions.
correctQuery: WITH monthly_rank AS (SELECT art_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', added_date) as mon, RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC('month', added_date) ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) as rnk FROM songs JOIN playlists USING (song_id) GROUP BY 1, 2) SELECT art_id FROM (SELECT art_id, rnk, LAG(rnk) OVER(PARTITION BY art_id ORDER BY mon) as p1, LAG(rnk, 2) OVER(PARTITION BY art_id ORDER BY mon) as p2 FROM monthly_rank) t WHERE rnk < p1 AND p1 < p2;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE artists (art_id INT); CREATE TABLE songs (song_id INT, art_id INT); CREATE TABLE playlists (list_id INT, song_id INT, added_date TIMESTAMP);

title: LMS Learning Path Acceleration
scenario: Calculate the average acceleration of completion (speeding up or slowing down) between successive lessons for each student.
tableSchema: progress (stu_id INT, lesson_id INT, completion_date DATE)
hint: Calculate delta time between lessons, then delta of deltas.
correctQuery: SELECT stu_id, AVG(diff_delta) FROM (SELECT stu_id, (diff - LAG(diff) OVER(PARTITION BY stu_id ORDER BY completion_date)) as diff_delta FROM (SELECT stu_id, (completion_date - LAG(completion_date) OVER(PARTITION BY stu_id ORDER BY completion_date)) as diff FROM progress) t) t2 GROUP BY stu_id;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE progress (stu_id INT, lesson_id INT, completion_date DATE);

title: Municipal Stadium High-Traffic Spikes
scenario: Identify records where the stadium hosted 100 or more people for at least three consecutive IDs. Return the result table ordered by visit_date in ascending order.
tableSchema: stadium (id INT, visit_date DATE, people INT)
hint: Use ROW_NUMBER() to create a grouping key (difference of ID and row number) to identify consecutive sequences, then filter groups with count >= 3.
correctQuery: WITH ConsecutiveGroups AS (SELECT id, visit_date, people, (id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id)) as grp FROM stadium WHERE people >= 100) SELECT id, visit_date, people FROM ConsecutiveGroups WHERE grp IN (SELECT grp FROM ConsecutiveGroups GROUP BY grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3) ORDER BY visit_date ASC;

title: Cloud Server Load Stability Anomaly
scenario: A 'Stability Anomaly' is defined as any server reporting CPU load > 85% for four or more consecutive reporting cycles, ignoring timestamp gaps. Retrieve the server_id, cycle_id, and cpu_load for all cycles participating in such an anomaly, ordered by cycle_id.
tableSchema: server_logs (server_id INT, cycle_id INT, cpu_load NUMERIC)
hint: Use PARTITION BY server_id with the difference-of-row-numbers technique to isolate streaks for each specific server.
correctQuery: WITH AnomalyIslands AS (SELECT server_id, cycle_id, cpu_load, (cycle_id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY server_id ORDER BY cycle_id)) as island_id FROM server_logs WHERE cpu_load > 85) SELECT server_id, cycle_id, cpu_load FROM AnomalyIslands WHERE (server_id, island_id) IN (SELECT server_id, island_id FROM AnomalyIslands GROUP BY server_id, island_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4) ORDER BY server_id, cycle_id;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE server_logs (server_id INT, cycle_id INT, cpu_load NUMERIC);

title: Stock Market Hot Streak Identification
scenario: Identify 'Hot Streaks' as assets that closed with a positive percentage gain for at least five consecutive trading days. Return ticker_symbol, trade_date, and percentage_change for all days within such streaks.
tableSchema: stock_history (ticker_symbol VARCHAR, trade_date DATE, percentage_change NUMERIC)
hint: Use two window functions: one for total rank and one for rank within positive-gain subset, then subtract to form grouping islands.
correctQuery: WITH StreakCalculations AS (SELECT ticker_symbol, trade_date, percentage_change, (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ticker_symbol ORDER BY trade_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ticker_symbol, CASE WHEN percentage_change > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END ORDER BY trade_date)) as streak_grp FROM stock_history) SELECT ticker_symbol, trade_date, percentage_change FROM StreakCalculations WHERE percentage_change > 0 AND (ticker_symbol, streak_grp) IN (SELECT ticker_symbol, streak_grp FROM StreakCalculations WHERE percentage_change > 0 GROUP BY ticker_symbol, streak_grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5) ORDER BY ticker_symbol, trade_date;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE stock_history (ticker_symbol VARCHAR, trade_date DATE, percentage_change NUMERIC);

title: Logistics Reliability Metric
scenario: Calculate the daily service disruption rate for a ride-hailing network. The metric is defined as the ratio of failed requests (driver or rider initiated) to total requests, specifically excluding participants currently flagged as 'banned' in our system. Focus on the date range '2013-10-01' to '2013-10-03'.
tableSchema: trips (trip_id INT, rider_id INT, driver_id INT, status VARCHAR, request_date DATE), users (user_id INT, is_banned BOOLEAN)
hint: Filter the trips table using a join or subquery on the users table to exclude banned accounts, then aggregate by request_date using conditional sum.
correctQuery: SELECT request_date as Day, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN status != 'completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)::NUMERIC / COUNT(*), 2) as "Cancellation Rate" FROM trips t JOIN users u1 ON t.rider_id = u1.user_id JOIN users u2 ON t.driver_id = u2.user_id WHERE u1.is_banned = FALSE AND u2.is_banned = FALSE AND request_date BETWEEN '2013-10-01' AND '2013-10-03' GROUP BY request_date;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE trips (trip_id INT, rider_id INT, driver_id INT, status VARCHAR, request_date DATE); CREATE TABLE users (user_id INT, is_banned BOOLEAN);

title: Driver Capacity Utilization Trend
scenario: Identify drivers who maintained a > 90% completion rate for 5 consecutive days.
tableSchema: trips (driver_id INT, status VARCHAR, request_date DATE)
hint: Aggregate daily completion rates, then use the difference-of-row-numbers technique to find islands.
correctQuery: WITH DailyStats AS (SELECT driver_id, request_date, COUNT(*) as total, SUM(CASE WHEN status='completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as comp FROM trips GROUP BY 1, 2), CompletionRates AS (SELECT driver_id, request_date, (comp::NUMERIC/total) as rate FROM DailyStats) SELECT driver_id FROM (SELECT driver_id, request_date, (ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY driver_id ORDER BY request_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY driver_id, CASE WHEN rate > 0.9 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END ORDER BY request_date)) as grp FROM CompletionRates WHERE rate > 0.9) t GROUP BY driver_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE trips (driver_id INT, status VARCHAR, request_date DATE);

title: Geographic Demand Surge
scenario: Find cities that experienced a 'Demand Surge' (views > 150% of the 30-day moving average) for more than 3 non-consecutive days in a month.
tableSchema: trips (city_id INT, request_date DATE)
hint: Use RANGE frames for moving averages.
correctQuery: WITH DailyDemand AS (SELECT city_id, request_date, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM trips GROUP BY 1, 2), MovingAvg AS (SELECT city_id, request_date, cnt, AVG(cnt) OVER(PARTITION BY city_id ORDER BY request_date RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '30 days' PRECEDING AND INTERVAL '1 day' PRECEDING) as avg_30 FROM DailyDemand) SELECT city_id FROM MovingAvg WHERE cnt > 1.5 * avg_30 GROUP BY city_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE trips (city_id INT, request_date DATE);

title: Churned User Re-engagement
scenario: Identify users who did not book a trip for at least 30 days and then completed at least 5 trips in the following 7 days.
tableSchema: trips (rider_id INT, request_date DATE)
hint: Use LEAD/LAG to find inactivity gaps, then join with aggregate counts.
correctQuery: WITH Gaps AS (SELECT rider_id, request_date, LAG(request_date) OVER(PARTITION BY rider_id ORDER BY request_date) as prev_date FROM trips) SELECT DISTINCT g.rider_id FROM Gaps g JOIN trips t ON g.rider_id = t.rider_id WHERE (g.request_date - g.prev_date) >= 30 AND t.request_date BETWEEN g.request_date AND g.request_date + INTERVAL '7 days' GROUP BY g.rider_id, g.request_date HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE trips (rider_id INT, request_date DATE);

title: Driver Revenue Volatility
scenario: Calculate the rolling standard deviation of daily earnings for drivers over a 14-day window.
tableSchema: trips (driver_id INT, fare NUMERIC, request_date DATE)
hint: Use STDDEV() OVER() with a range frame.
correctQuery: SELECT driver_id, request_date, STDDEV(daily_fare) OVER(PARTITION BY driver_id ORDER BY request_date RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '14 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM (SELECT driver_id, request_date, SUM(fare) as daily_fare FROM trips GROUP BY 1, 2) t;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE trips (driver_id INT, fare NUMERIC, request_date DATE);

title: Peak Hour Congestion Detection
scenario: Identify the top 3 hours of the day (by request count) for each city that contribute to > 40% of the city's daily demand.
tableSchema: trips (city_id INT, request_date DATE, request_hour INT)
hint: Calculate hourly count vs total daily count per city.
correctQuery: WITH HourlyCnt AS (SELECT city_id, request_date, request_hour, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM trips GROUP BY 1,2,3), Stats AS (SELECT *, SUM(cnt) OVER(PARTITION BY city_id, request_date) as daily_tot FROM HourlyCnt) SELECT city_id, request_hour FROM Stats WHERE cnt::NUMERIC / daily_tot > 0.4 ORDER BY city_id, cnt DESC;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE trips (city_id INT, request_date DATE, request_hour INT);

title: Cross-Platform Loyalty
scenario: Find users whose average trip frequency has increased consistently every quarter for the last two years.
tableSchema: trips (rider_id INT, request_date DATE)
hint: Aggregate by rider/quarter, then use LAG to compare 8 consecutive periods.
correctQuery: WITH QStats AS (SELECT rider_id, DATE_TRUNC('quarter', request_date) as qtr, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM trips GROUP BY 1, 2) SELECT rider_id FROM (SELECT rider_id, cnt, LAG(cnt, 1) OVER(PARTITION BY rider_id ORDER BY qtr) as p1, ... FROM QStats) t WHERE cnt > p1 AND p1 > p2 AND ...;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE trips (rider_id INT, request_date DATE);

title: Driver Idle Time Estimation
scenario: Calculate the average 'gap' between a driver's completed trip and their next pickup time.
tableSchema: trips (driver_id INT, pickup_time TIMESTAMP, dropoff_time TIMESTAMP)
hint: Use LEAD() on pickup_time and compare with current dropoff_time.
correctQuery: SELECT driver_id, AVG(pickup_time - dropoff_time) FROM (SELECT driver_id, pickup_time, dropoff_time, LEAD(pickup_time) OVER(PARTITION BY driver_id ORDER BY dropoff_time) as next_pickup FROM trips) t WHERE next_pickup IS NOT NULL GROUP BY driver_id;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE trips (driver_id INT, pickup_time TIMESTAMP, dropoff_time TIMESTAMP);

title: Market Saturation Index
scenario: Identify cities where the ratio of 'active' drivers to 'active' riders has dropped below 0.1 for 3 consecutive days.
tableSchema: trips (city_id INT, driver_id INT, rider_id INT, request_date DATE)
hint: Count distinct drivers and riders daily, then compare ratio.
correctQuery: WITH DailyActivity AS (SELECT city_id, request_date, COUNT(DISTINCT driver_id) as d_cnt, COUNT(DISTINCT rider_id) as r_cnt FROM trips GROUP BY 1, 2) SELECT city_id FROM (SELECT city_id, request_date, (d_cnt::NUMERIC/r_cnt) as ratio, LAG(d_cnt::NUMERIC/r_cnt, 1) OVER(PARTITION BY city_id ORDER BY request_date) as p1, LAG(d_cnt::NUMERIC/r_cnt, 2) OVER(PARTITION BY city_id ORDER BY request_date) as p2 FROM DailyActivity) t WHERE ratio < 0.1 AND p1 < 0.1 AND p2 < 0.1;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE trips (city_id INT, driver_id INT, rider_id INT, request_date DATE);

title: Ride-Hailing Fraud Detection
scenario: Detect 'Rapid Cycling' fraud: Find drivers who completed more than 5 trips in under 1 hour in a single day.
tableSchema: trips (driver_id INT, pickup_time TIMESTAMP, dropoff_time TIMESTAMP)
hint: Self-join or use window frame range to count trips in 1-hour window.
correctQuery: SELECT driver_id, pickup_time::DATE FROM (SELECT driver_id, pickup_time, COUNT(*) OVER(PARTITION BY driver_id ORDER BY pickup_time RANGE BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND INTERVAL '1 hour' FOLLOWING) as trip_count FROM trips) t WHERE trip_count > 5;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE trips (driver_id INT, pickup_time TIMESTAMP, dropoff_time TIMESTAMP);

title: Social Network Connectivity Analysis
scenario: You are managing a professional networking platform. Analyze the 'RequestAccepted' logs to identify the user who holds the highest number of unique connections. A connection is established when either a request is sent by an requester or received by an accepter. Determine the user ID with the maximum total connections and the corresponding count of those connections.
tableSchema: RequestAccepted (requester_id INT, accepter_id INT, accept_date DATE)
hint: Since connections are bidirectional, combine requester_id and accepter_id into a single stream using UNION ALL, then aggregate the counts per ID and select the record with the maximum total.
correctQuery: WITH AllConnections AS (SELECT requester_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted UNION ALL SELECT accepter_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted), ConnectionCounts AS (SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS num FROM AllConnections GROUP BY id) SELECT id, num FROM ConnectionCounts ORDER BY num DESC LIMIT 1;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE RequestAccepted (requester_id INT, accepter_id INT, accept_date DATE); INSERT INTO RequestAccepted VALUES (1, 2, '2016-06-03'), (1, 3, '2016-06-08'), (2, 3, '2016-06-08'), (3, 4, '2016-06-09');

title: Dynamic Seat Reassignment
scenario: You are organizing a seminar where students are seated in an ordered row based on their registration ID. To encourage interaction, you decide to swap the seat assignments for every pair of adjacent students. If the total number of students is odd, the student in the final position must remain in their original seat. Provide a list of students mapped to their newly assigned IDs, ensuring the final output is sorted by ID in ascending order.
tableSchema: Seat (id INT, student VARCHAR)
hint: Use the CASE statement to reassign IDs: if an ID is odd and not the last record, add 1; if an ID is even, subtract 1. You can identify the last record using a subquery for the total count.
correctQuery: SELECT CASE WHEN id % 2 != 0 AND id = (SELECT MAX(id) FROM Seat) THEN id WHEN id % 2 != 0 THEN id + 1 ELSE id - 1 END AS id, student FROM Seat ORDER BY id ASC;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Seat (id INT PRIMARY KEY, student VARCHAR); INSERT INTO Seat VALUES (1, 'Abbot'), (2, 'Doris'), (3, 'Emerson'), (4, 'Green'), (5, 'Jeames');

title: Inventory Supply Chain Rebalancing
scenario: You are the supply chain manager for a warehouse where items are stored in numbered storage bins (ID 1 through N). To optimize retrieval paths, you must swap the item assignments between every adjacent pair of storage bins. If there is an odd number of bins, the item in the highest-numbered bin must remain in its original position. Generate a report mapping each item to its newly assigned bin ID, ensuring the output is ordered by bin ID in ascending order.
tableSchema: Inventory (bin_id INT, item_name VARCHAR)
hint: Use a CASE statement combined with a subquery to find the total number of bins. Map odd bin IDs to ID+1 (unless it is the final bin) and even bin IDs to ID-1.
correctQuery: SELECT CASE WHEN bin_id % 2 != 0 AND bin_id = (SELECT MAX(bin_id) FROM Inventory) THEN bin_id WHEN bin_id % 2 != 0 THEN bin_id + 1 ELSE bin_id - 1 END AS bin_id, item_name FROM Inventory ORDER BY bin_id ASC;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Inventory (bin_id INT PRIMARY KEY, item_name VARCHAR); INSERT INTO Inventory VALUES (1, 'Widget_A'), (2, 'Widget_B'), (3, 'Widget_C'), (4, 'Widget_D'), (5, 'Widget_E');

title: Network Node Traffic Redirection
scenario: In a distributed network, traffic flows through nodes assigned sequential IDs. Due to a load-balancing maintenance event, you are required to rotate the traffic routing of every pair of consecutive nodes. If the node sequence ends with an odd count, the final node in the sequence must maintain its original routing assignment. Produce a list of nodes with their adjusted routing IDs, maintaining ascending order of the new node ID.
tableSchema: NetworkNodes (node_id INT, traffic_type VARCHAR)
hint: Calculate the parity of the node_id. If a node is at an odd position and is not the tail of the sequence, increment its ID. If it is at an even position, decrement its ID.
correctQuery: SELECT CASE WHEN node_id % 2 != 0 AND node_id = (SELECT MAX(node_id) FROM NetworkNodes) THEN node_id WHEN node_id % 2 != 0 THEN node_id + 1 ELSE node_id - 1 END AS node_id, traffic_type FROM NetworkNodes ORDER BY node_id ASC;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE NetworkNodes (node_id INT PRIMARY KEY, traffic_type VARCHAR); INSERT INTO NetworkNodes VALUES (1, 'Voice'), (2, 'Data'), (3, 'Video'), (4, 'SMS'), (5, 'IoT');

title: Digital Asset Priority Swapping
scenario: You are organizing a playlist of digital assets where each asset is assigned a sequential rank (1 to N). To test varying user engagement based on placement, you are tasked with swapping the ranks of every two consecutive assets. Should the total number of assets be an odd number, the asset at the final rank must remain unchanged. Output the final table showing the new rank and the asset name, sorted by rank.
tableSchema: DigitalAssets (rank_id INT, asset_name VARCHAR)
hint: Identify the total count of assets to handle the odd-number edge case. Use the modulo operator on the rank_id to perform the conditional swap.
correctQuery: SELECT CASE WHEN rank_id % 2 != 0 AND rank_id = (SELECT MAX(rank_id) FROM DigitalAssets) THEN rank_id WHEN rank_id % 2 != 0 THEN rank_id + 1 ELSE rank_id - 1 END AS rank_id, asset_name FROM DigitalAssets ORDER BY rank_id ASC;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE DigitalAssets (rank_id INT PRIMARY KEY, asset_name VARCHAR); INSERT INTO DigitalAssets VALUES (1, 'Podcast_01'), (2, 'Podcast_02'), (3, 'Podcast_03'), (4, 'Podcast_04'), (5, 'Podcast_05');

title: Prolific Reviewer & High-Engagement Temporal Analysis
scenario: You are a lead architect for a film analytics platform. Perform two specific tasks: 1) Identify the user who has contributed the most reviews; if a tie occurs, select the name that appears first alphabetically. 2) Identify the movie that received the highest average rating specifically during the 'February 2020' window. If multiple movies share the same highest average, select the one with the lexicographically smallest title. Combine these results into a single output column named 'results'.
tableSchema: Movies (movie_id INT, title VARCHAR), Users (user_id INT, name VARCHAR), MovieRating (movie_id INT, user_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE)
hint: Use two separate UNION ALL subqueries. For the first part, join Users with MovieRating and order by count descending and name ascending. For the second, filter by date range, join with Movies, group by title, and order by avg(rating) descending and title ascending.
correctQuery: (SELECT u.name AS results FROM Users u JOIN MovieRating mr ON u.user_id = mr.user_id GROUP BY u.name ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, u.name ASC LIMIT 1) UNION ALL (SELECT m.title AS results FROM Movies m JOIN MovieRating mr ON m.movie_id = mr.movie_id WHERE mr.created_at >= '2020-02-01' AND mr.created_at <= '2020-02-29' GROUP BY m.title ORDER BY AVG(mr.rating) DESC, m.title ASC LIMIT 1);
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Movies (movie_id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE Users (user_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE MovieRating (movie_id INT, user_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE);

title: Super-User Contribution Velocity
scenario: Identify 'super-reviewers'—those who have submitted at least 3 reviews in a single calendar month. For these users, calculate their average rating provided during that specific month. Return the user name and the month (in YYYY-MM format) where they achieved this engagement level, ordered by their average rating in descending order.
tableSchema: Users (user_id INT, name VARCHAR), MovieRating (user_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE)
hint: Group by user_id and month, filter for count >= 3, then calculate average rating.
correctQuery: SELECT u.name, TO_CHAR(mr.created_at, 'YYYY-MM') as review_month, AVG(mr.rating) as avg_rating FROM Users u JOIN MovieRating mr ON u.user_id = mr.user_id GROUP BY u.name, review_month HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 ORDER BY avg_rating DESC;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Users (user_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE MovieRating (user_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE);

title: Genre Sentiment Decay
scenario: Analyze the 'sentiment decay' of movies by comparing the average rating of a movie in the first 30 days after its release versus the average rating received after 90 days post-release. Return the movie title and the difference in average ratings (First_30_Days_Avg - After_90_Days_Avg), sorted by the highest rating drop.
tableSchema: Movies (movie_id INT, title VARCHAR), MovieRating (movie_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE)
hint: Use conditional aggregation (FILTER) to calculate two separate averages for each movie based on the date range.
correctQuery: SELECT m.title, AVG(mr.rating) FILTER (WHERE mr.created_at <= '2020-01-30') - AVG(mr.rating) FILTER (WHERE mr.created_at > '2020-03-31') as rating_delta FROM Movies m JOIN MovieRating mr ON m.movie_id = mr.movie_id GROUP BY m.title HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 ORDER BY rating_delta DESC;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Movies (movie_id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE MovieRating (movie_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE);

title: Reviewer Consensus Variance
scenario: Calculate the consensus variance for every movie that has at least 5 reviews. The consensus variance is defined as the standard deviation of all ratings for that movie. Return the title of the movie and its rating standard deviation, ordered from the most divisive (highest variance) to the most consensus-driven (lowest variance).
tableSchema: Movies (movie_id INT, title VARCHAR), MovieRating (movie_id INT, rating INT)
hint: Join Movies with MovieRating, group by title, and use the STDDEV() function on the ratings.
correctQuery: SELECT m.title, STDDEV(mr.rating) as rating_stddev FROM Movies m JOIN MovieRating mr ON m.movie_id = mr.movie_id GROUP BY m.title HAVING COUNT(mr.rating) >= 5 ORDER BY rating_stddev DESC;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Movies (movie_id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE MovieRating (movie_id INT, rating INT);

title: Consecutive High-Rating streaks
scenario: Identify movies that have received a rating of 5 (the highest score) for at least 3 consecutive reviews in the database, ordered chronologically by 'created_at'. Return the movie title and the dates of the first and last reviews in such streaks.
tableSchema: Movies (movie_id INT, title VARCHAR), MovieRating (movie_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE)
hint: Use the difference of row numbers technique to identify consecutive rating islands.
correctQuery: WITH RatingIslands AS (SELECT m.title, mr.created_at, (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY m.title ORDER BY mr.created_at) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY m.title, (CASE WHEN mr.rating = 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ORDER BY mr.created_at)) as island_id FROM Movies m JOIN MovieRating mr ON m.movie_id = mr.movie_id) SELECT title, MIN(created_at), MAX(created_at) FROM RatingIslands GROUP BY title, island_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Movies (movie_id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE MovieRating (movie_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE);

title: Monthly Revenue Attribution and Growth
scenario: As a data analyst, you are tasked with identifying the 'Top Performer' for each month. A performer is defined as the user with the highest total rating sum in a given month. Output the result in a table with two columns: 'month' (in YYYY-MM format) and 'top_user_name'. If there is a tie in the total rating sum, select the user name that is lexicographically smaller.
tableSchema: Users (user_id INT, name VARCHAR), MovieRating (user_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE)
hint: Use TO_CHAR() to extract the month, group by month and user, calculate the SUM(rating), and use RANK() or a subquery with ORDER BY to find the top user per month.
correctQuery: WITH MonthlyScores AS (SELECT TO_CHAR(created_at, 'YYYY-MM') as month, u.name, SUM(rating) as total_score FROM Users u JOIN MovieRating mr ON u.user_id = mr.user_id GROUP BY 1, 2), RankedScores AS (SELECT month, name, RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY month ORDER BY total_score DESC, name ASC) as rnk FROM MonthlyScores) SELECT month, name AS top_user_name FROM RankedScores WHERE rnk = 1 ORDER BY month ASC;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Users (user_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE MovieRating (user_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE);

title: Movie Rating Velocity Trend
scenario: Analyze the 'rating velocity' for each movie. Output a table with three columns: 'movie_title', 'review_date', and 'cumulative_avg_rating'. The cumulative average should be calculated for each movie ordered by date. Ensure the output is sorted by movie_title then review_date.
tableSchema: Movies (movie_id INT, title VARCHAR), MovieRating (movie_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE)
hint: Join the tables and use the AVG() window function partitioned by movie_id, ordered by created_at, to compute the rolling mean.
correctQuery: SELECT m.title AS movie_title, mr.created_at AS review_date, AVG(mr.rating) OVER(PARTITION BY m.movie_id ORDER BY mr.created_at) AS cumulative_avg_rating FROM Movies m JOIN MovieRating mr ON m.movie_id = mr.movie_id ORDER BY movie_title, review_date;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Movies (movie_id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE MovieRating (movie_id INT, rating INT, created_at DATE);

title: User Discrepancy Flagging
scenario: Identify users whose individual rating for a specific movie deviates from that movie's overall average rating by more than 2 points. Output the 'user_name', 'movie_title', and the 'deviation_score'.
tableSchema: Users (user_id INT, name VARCHAR), Movies (movie_id INT, title VARCHAR), MovieRating (user_id INT, movie_id INT, rating INT)
hint: Use a CTE to calculate the average rating per movie, then join it back to the main MovieRating table to calculate the absolute difference.
correctQuery: WITH MovieAverages AS (SELECT movie_id, AVG(rating) as avg_rating FROM MovieRating GROUP BY movie_id) SELECT u.name AS user_name, m.title AS movie_title, ABS(mr.rating - ma.avg_rating) AS deviation_score FROM MovieRating mr JOIN Users u ON mr.user_id = u.user_id JOIN Movies m ON mr.movie_id = m.movie_id JOIN MovieAverages ma ON mr.movie_id = ma.movie_id WHERE ABS(mr.rating - ma.avg_rating) > 2 ORDER BY deviation_score DESC;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Users (user_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE Movies (movie_id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE MovieRating (user_id INT, movie_id INT, rating INT);

title: Engagement Drought Analysis
scenario: An 'engagement drought' is defined as any period where a movie receives no ratings for at least 7 consecutive days. Output the 'movie_title', 'start_drought_date', and 'end_drought_date' for every drought period longer than 7 days.
tableSchema: Movies (movie_id INT, title VARCHAR), MovieRating (movie_id INT, created_at DATE)
hint: Identify gaps by comparing the current review date with the next review date using LEAD(). Calculate the interval of these gaps.
correctQuery: WITH ReviewGaps AS (SELECT movie_id, created_at, LEAD(created_at) OVER(PARTITION BY movie_id ORDER BY created_at) as next_review FROM MovieRating) SELECT m.title AS movie_title, created_at + INTERVAL '1 day' AS start_drought_date, next_review - INTERVAL '1 day' AS end_drought_date FROM ReviewGaps rg JOIN Movies m ON rg.movie_id = m.movie_id WHERE (next_review - created_at) > 7;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Movies (movie_id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE MovieRating (movie_id INT, created_at DATE);

title: User-Movie Rating Pair Consistency
scenario: Find pairs of users (user1_name, user2_name) who have rated the exact same set of movies with the exact same ratings. Output unique pairs where user1_id < user2_id.
tableSchema: Users (user_id INT, name VARCHAR), MovieRating (user_id INT, movie_id INT, rating INT)
hint: Aggregate the movies and ratings into an array per user using ARRAY_AGG(), sort the arrays, and perform an INNER JOIN on these arrays.
correctQuery: WITH UserRatings AS (SELECT user_id, ARRAY_AGG(movie_id || ':' || rating ORDER BY movie_id) as profile FROM MovieRating GROUP BY user_id) SELECT u1.name AS user1_name, u2.name AS user2_name FROM UserRatings ur1 JOIN UserRatings ur2 ON ur1.profile = ur2.profile AND ur1.user_id < ur2.user_id JOIN Users u1 ON ur1.user_id = u1.user_id JOIN Users u2 ON ur2.user_id = u2.user_id;
setupSQL: CREATE TABLE Users (user_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR); CREATE TABLE MovieRating (user_id INT, movie_id INT, rating INT);
